edinburgh.blurb: Built on an extinct volcano and split by a ravine, Scotland's capital is all dark stone, sudden closes of light, and a literary habit of putting the view to work. The castle sits on an extinct volcano; the New Town below it was laid out in the 1760s and still reads as one coherent idea.
edinburgh.goWhen: May to September; the festivals are August, the lights are the first week of January

london.blurb: Two thousand years of settlement stacked on top of each other, and the point of a visit is not the list of sights but the fabric between them. Every bridge and market here has an argument about it, which is why asking a local beats reading a list.
london.goWhen: April to June and September to October

dublin.blurb: A compact, walkable capital of Georgian squares and pub doors, on a bay that turns the whole city toward the water. Literary Dublin is real but the pubs are better: the city has one of the highest densities of live music in Europe.

killary-fjord.blurb: Ireland's deepest fjord, twenty minutes off the Ring of Kerry road and almost entirely undeveloped. The cable car up the mountain and the boat cruise into the fjord are the two reasons to leave the coastal road for it.
killary-fjord.goWhen: May to September; it is a wet, changeable place year-round

reykjavik.blurb: The world's northernmost capital of a country, which is why everything in it is either geothermal, painted in corrugated iron, or both. From the harbour you can see the glaciers, and in winter the aurora is a genuine possibility rather than a brochure claim.
reykjavik.goWhen: June to August for midnight sun; September to March for the aurora

bruges.blurb: A medieval trading city barely larger than its own centre, where canals run between brick gables and the only serious traffic is bicycles. The high-impact car-free zone covers most of what visitors want to see.
bruges.goWhen: April to June and September to October; December has a famous Christmas market

amsterdam.blurb: A city built on piles, laid out in a semicircle of canals, and defended by being exactly flat and exactly open. More than 800 bridges and a houseboat culture that is a way of life rather than a tourist attraction.
amsterdam.goWhen: April to May and September; the flower fields around the city are April only

paris.blurb: Everyone gets the Louvre. The better Paris is in the markets, the small museums, and the arrondissements one metro stop from where everyone else is not. The city is a set of 20 distinct neighbourhoods that happen to share a postcode.
paris.goWhen: May and September to October; the Parisians leave in August

route-de-napoleon.blurb: A 260-kilometre road climbing from the Mediterranean to the Alps, planted with monuments in 1821 and kept passable for cyclists ever since. It is a cycling road before it is a pilgrimage, and the switchbacks on the Col de Vars are the honest part.
route-de-napoleon.goWhen: June to September, before the alpine snow returns

zermatt.blurb: A car-free village at the foot of the Matterhorn, reached only by a narrow-gauge train, cable car or on foot. The peak is the reason, but the valley is the reason people stay past the photograph.
zermatt.goWhen: Late June to September for hiking; December to March for skiing

berlin.blurb: A city assembled from other cities' rubble, which explains the density of walls, murals and unfinished buildings. Its culture operates on a 24-hour clock and treats the alternative scene as a mainstream industry rather than an undercurrent.
bestFor: Street art and the remaining Wall
berlin.goWhen: May to September; December for the markets and the lights

dessau.blurb: The city Walter Gropius built in the 1920s to house the Bauhaus, and the clearest statement anywhere that design is a social programme rather than a look. It is a working pilot project on a grey river, not a museum set-piece.
dessau.goWhen: April to October; the school tours run through the week

prague.blurb: A city of spires and cellars, where the beer is cheaper than the water and the river is the only free view of the skyline. The Castle District sits above a medieval grid that survived four centuries largely because commerce was here, not monuments.
prague.goWhen: April to June and September to October

krakow.blurb: Poland's former capital, and the only major medieval city in the country that was never destroyed, which is why its Old Town is intact rather than reconstructed. Kazimierz, the old Jewish quarter, has its own separate and harder history.
krakow.goWhen: April to June and September to October; December for the markets

vienna.blurb: An imperial capital that went out of business gracefully, leaving coffee houses, wine cellars and 1,600 public buildings nobody had to demolish. The city is a UNESCO listing in its entirety, which sounds like hyperbole until you try to list what is excluded.
bestFor: The Danube and the Schloss Belvedere
vienna.goWhen: April to June and September to December

budapest.blurb: Two cities on one river, Buda in the hills and Pest on the flat, joined by the Chain Bridge and thermal baths that the Romans started. Ruin bars, an enormous market hall, and a ruin pub scene with more honesty per square metre than most cities manage.
budapest.goWhen: April to June and September to October

sibenik.blurb: A UNESCO-listed stone city on the Croatian coast, and the birthplace of Croatia's football and basketball culture. Much of the old town was built entirely from stone, including the roof of St James Cathedral, which is a UNESCO first.

dubrovnik.blurb: A walled city of terracotta roofs on a cliff, encircled by 1,940 metres of medieval fortifications. It is beautiful and it is managed: the old town's street furniture is regulated, cruise crowds arrive in waves, and the honest advice is to come early.
dubrovnik.goWhen: April to June and September to October; July and August are intense

rome.blurb: A layered city: the Colosseum, then Baroque, then the trattoria where the same family has been making cacio e pepe since before the war. It is also a working modern city, and the food is the free part.
rome.goWhen: April to June and September to October; avoid August

the-veneto.blurb: Italy's northeast corner, a flat river plain of Palladian villas, Prosecco hills and walled cities that are almost empty of tourists. Venice gets the crowds; the Veneto is where they were before Venice became a cruise port.
the-veneto.goWhen: April to June and September to October; July for the opera season

aeolian-islands.blurb: Seven volcanic islands north of Sicily, two of which are still erupting, and the only UNESCO site in Europe recognised for its geology rather than its architecture. Vulcano has the black sand beaches; Stromboli has the volcano you can walk up to at dusk.
aeolian-islands.goWhen: May to June and September to October; the ferries thin out in winter

athens.blurb: A city built on seven hills with the Acropolis on the highest one, layered with Roman, Byzantine and Ottoman Athens under the modern capital. The best surviving ancient urban planning in Greece is in the streets around the Agora, not on the rock above it.
athens.goWhen: April to June and September to October; July and August are hot and crowded

aegean-sea.blurb: The sea itself rather than any one island, and the reason Greece reads as an archipelago from a map. Cycladic whitewash, Dodecanese green, the volcanic arc running from Santorini to Nisyros, and ferry schedules that decide what is actually possible.
aegean-sea.goWhen: May to June for full service, September for warm water and no crowds

barcelona.blurb: A grid city with a sea at one end and mountains at the other, built on a theory that cities can be made better by design. The Gothic Quarter is a postcard, but the neighbourhoods beyond Eixample and Gràcia are where the city actually eats and drinks.
barcelona.goWhen: April to June and September to October; avoid the August heat

granada.blurb: The Alhambra is the headline, but Granada is what the Alhambra looks like from — the Nasrid palaces on the Sabika hill, the Albaicín whitewashed quarter opposite, and flamenco bars that do not perform for tourists on a schedule.
granada.goWhen: April to June and September to October; book the Alhambra weeks ahead

lisbon.blurb: Draped over seven hills above the Tagus, Lisbon is all pastel facades, blue-tiled churches, tram bells, and a pastry counter worth getting up early for. The best food is the cheapest: go where the queue is all one language.
bestFor: A long lunch on the river
lisbon.goWhen: March to May and September to October

porto.blurb: Portugal's second city, built on granite above the Douro, where the old town is tiled, steep and unashamedly mercantile. Port lodges, riverside cellars and a food culture that is a cheaper and more serious version of Lisbon's.
bestFor: Ribeira and the Dom Luís I bridge
porto.goWhen: April to June and September to October

skanor-falsterbo.blurb: The southern tip of Sweden, where the Baltic meets the Øresund and the light comes off the water like nothing else in Scandinavia. A medieval fishing village, a 1940s art colony, and one of the best birdwatching spots on the continent.
skanor-falsterbo.goWhen: May and June for long light, September and October for migrating birds

saint-cuthbert-s-way.blurb: A 62-kilometre coast path from Melrose to Holy Island, following the route of a 7th-century pilgrim who walked barefoot. It runs on the edge of the Northumberland coast, past Lindisfarne's tidal causeway, and it is the finest linear walk in England.
saint-cuthbert-s-way.goWhen: May to September; check the tide tables for the causeway crossing

the-tweed.blurb: The river that gives Scotland its name, running from Tweed's Well in the Borders to the North Sea, and the source of the famous tweed cloth. Much of it is catch-and-release trout fishing rather than scenery, which makes it a destination for a specific and committed kind of visitor.
the-tweed.goWhen: May to September for walking; September for the salmon season

cairo.blurb: A city of 20 million on the Nile that has been a capital in some form for five thousand years, and still has the largest collection of medieval Islamic architecture in the world in its eastern cemetery district. Islamic Cairo is a UNESCO listing of a working city, not a ruin.
cairo.goWhen: October to April; the summer heat is genuinely dangerous

marrakech.blurb: A red-walled city of riads, souks and a 12th-century kasbah, in the foothills of the High Atlas a day's drive from the desert. The medina is genuinely disorienting and the reason to hire a local guide rather than a map.
bestFor: A hammam that is not a tourist show
marrakech.goWhen: March to May and September to November

rabat.blurb: Morocco's capital rather than its best-known city, and a quieter answer than Marrakech. The Kasbah of the Udayas sits on a rock at the mouth of the Bou Regreg with views across to Chellah and the Rabat-Salé medinas.
rabat.goWhen: March to May and September to November

cape-town.blurb: A city between a mountain and two oceans, which means you can be in a Table Mountain gallery and a surfing beach within the hour. It is expensive and it is unequal, and both facts shape what you should see and where.
bestFor: Table Mountain on a clear day
cape-town.goWhen: October to April for weather; December to mid-January is peak price

victoria-falls.blurb: The largest sheet of falling water on earth, sixteen kilometres wide at its widest, and a UNESCO listing shared with neighbouring Mosi-oa-Tunya in Zambia. The Zimbabwean side gives the view; the Zambian side lets you walk on the Knife-Edge bridge into the spray.
victoria-falls.goWhen: May to October; the falls are at full flow then and at their fiercest

gombe-national-park.blurb: The only place in the world with a guaranteed wild chimpanzee population, on the shore of Lake Victoria where the forest still meets the water. Research has run here since 1960, so habituation is genuine rather than staged.
gombe-national-park.goWhen: June to October and December to February; the rains close the trails

tsavo-national-parks.blurb: Two parks totalling 22,000 square kilometres, split by the Nairobi–Mombasa road, and for decades the elephant population of East Africa. Lion prides, the Shetani lava flows, and a red dust that gets into everything, permanently.
tsavo-national-parks.goWhen: June to October and January to February; avoid the long rains

sao-tome.blurb: A volcanic island in the Gulf of Guinea, halfway to the nearest continent, with 90% forest cover and a cacao economy that is still largely smallholder. It is the least visited country in the world and the reason the guide industry is community-owned.
sao-tome.goWhen: June to September and December to March; the wet season is short and green

istanbul.blurb: The only major city in the world sitting on two continents, and 1,500 years of this has produced a food culture with no rival. The Bosphorus ferries are the best commute in Europe and cost a fraction of a crossing.
istanbul.goWhen: April to June and September to October; January for snow

petra.blurb: A Nabataean city carved into rose sandstone canyons, reached by walking 800 metres through a natural slot that is designed to be narrower than the Treasury it frames. Two thousand years of abandonment have preserved it because nobody could rebuild it.
petra.goWhen: October to April; summer midday heat makes the Siq punishing

wadi-rum.blurb: A 10,000-year-old red desert of sandstone mountains and dune fields, and the best-preserved film-scape on earth. The Bedouin camps are the point: tea by the fire, no Wi-Fi, and the clearest night sky in the Middle East.
bestFor: Bedouin camp with no light pollution
wadi-rum.goWhen: March to May and September to November; cold nights, so bring a layer

oman.blurb: A country with a coastline on the Arabian Sea, a desert interior, and mountains that make it a hiking destination rather than just a transit stop. Wadi Shab has swimable freshwater pools an hour from the empty coast, which is the most surprising thing here.
bestFor: Dune driving in the Empty Quarter
oman.goWhen: October to April; the Dhofar khareef monsoon is June to September

abu-dhabi.blurb: The UAE capital rather than Dubai, and the one built around a marina and a race track instead of a skyline. The Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque and the Louvre Abu Dhabi are the reason to spend two days rather than a stopover hour.
abu-dhabi.goWhen: November to March; the summer is too hot to be outside

jaipur.blurb: Rajasthan's pink city, founded in 1727 and still defined by the colour scheme it was built in, with the Hawa Mahal and Amber Fort both a short trip out. Bazaars here are organised by craft, so you can buy in a single street rather than all day.
bestFor: Hawa Mahal from the rooftop opposite
Stepwells, of which there are many
jaipur.goWhen: October to March; the summer is genuinely too hot to walk

taj-mahal.blurb: A Mughal mausoleum built by an emperor for his wife over roughly twenty years, in white marble inlaid with semi-precious stone. It changes appearance entirely with the light and the season, from pink at dawn to gold at sunset, and the haze over the Yamuna can close the view for days.
bestFor: The mosque and the guest house across the river
taj-mahal.goWhen: October to March; buy tickets well ahead and enter at sunrise

varanasi.blurb: One of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world, on the Ganges, where the cremation ghats run continuously and the ritual is not a spectacle to be consumed but a life to be observed. The Ghatavasana on a new-moon morning is the largest human gathering on earth, and the city is at its most extraordinary.
varanasi.goWhen: October to March; the crowds at peak pilgrimage months are extreme

ranthambore.blurb: The most reliable place in India to see wild tigers, in a 1,000-square-kilometre national park of lakes, ruins and forest where the ruins date to the ninth century. Sightings are genuinely uncertain, which is the correct way to approach it.
bestFor: Wild tigers in forest, not a zoo
The Chittorgarh and Kumbhalgarh ruins in the park
ranthambore.goWhen: October to June; the park closes for the monsoon

goa.blurb: A state of beaches, Portuguese-era churches, and a hinterland of spice farms and the Western Ghats, which is the part most visitors never see. The south of the state is the quieter half, and the Dudhsagar Falls railway runs through the forest.
goa.goWhen: November to February; the monsoon breaks from June to September

kerala-backwaters.blurb: A 900-kilometre network of lakes and canals threaded through coconut and paddy, where a houseboat trip is the local form of a weekend. The canals run between Kumarakom and Alleppey, and the town of Alleppey is the centre of it.
bestFor: A dawn houseboat through the canals
kerala-backwaters.goWhen: November to March; the monsoon is heavy from June to August

darjeeling.blurb: A hill station in the eastern Himalaya where the air, the tea and the rail all date from the British Raj, and where the Toy Train still runs on a narrow gauge. Singbulli and Kalimpong are better than Darjeeling itself for an unhurried stay.
bestFor: The Toy Train on a UNESCO line
Tiger Hill for the Everest view
darjeeling.goWhen: October to December for clear Himalayan views; March to May for rhododendrons

gujarat.blurb: Western India's most distinctive state, and it is a textile state: block-printed, tie-dyed, embroidered, and mirror-worked cloth made in kutch and around Surat. Rani ki Vav in Patan is a stepwell built like a temple upside-down, and Modhera's Sun Temple predates Konark by five centuries.
bestFor: Bandhani and block printing in Kutch
gujarat.goWhen: November to February; the Rann is walkable only in the cool months

bangkok.blurb: Thailand's capital, built on a canal network over a floodplain, and a food culture that is more famous than its temples. The canal boats and the river still do the same work as the roads do elsewhere, and riding one is the best cheap tour in the city.
bestFor: Wat Pho and Wat Arun early
Talad Rot Fai and the Chatuchak weekend market
bangkok.goWhen: November to February; March to May is the heat haze

hanoi.blurb: Vietnam's capital, a lake-city of French colonial villas, tube houses and coffee served on a low stool. The Old Quarter is a grid of narrow streets organised around trades rather than addresses, and the coffee culture is genuinely a local habit, not a tourist theme.
bestFor: Egg coffee and ca phe sua da
hanoi.goWhen: October to December and February to April

danang.blurb: Vietnam's third city, between the Marble Mountains and a beach with a whole skyline of resort towers on it, and increasingly the base for central Vietnam. The old imperial city in Huế is two hours south and is the actual reason for this part of the coast.
bestFor: The tail of Hoi An and the old town
Ba Na Hills and the Golden Bridge
danang.goWhen: February to April and August to October; the typhoon season is roughly October to December

bali.blurb: An island of volcanic rice terraces, temple complexes, and a surf culture that came and went and left good waves behind. Ubud is the cliché and Sidemen is the answer, where the weaving, the coffee and the river still run the way they always have.
bali.goWhen: April to October is dry season; July and August are busiest and driest

singapore.blurb: A city-state that solved the things cities usually fail at, and can be defended about food, gardens, and housing as a result. Its hawker centres are UNESCO-listed, and the reason to go is to eat in them rather than in the restaurants.
bestFor: Hawker centres and their Michelin stalls
Gardens by the Bay at night
Losing a productive afternoon to a kopi
singapore.goWhen: February to April, the least humid stretch of the year

batang-ai-national-park.blurb: A 3,500-square-kilometre rain forest on Borneo with orangutans, hornbills, and a lake that was almost completely deforested in the 1960s and then given back. Its Iban and Orang Asli communities run the lodges and guides, which is the whole point of going.
batang-ai-national-park.goWhen: March to October; rain is possible year-round and nobody should be surprised

great-wall.blurb: Not one wall but many, built and rebuilt by successive dynasties over two thousand years, and mostly not the tourist section. Mutianyu and Jinshanling have original Ming brickwork and watchtowers; the restored ramparts at Badaling are the busy one.
bestFor: Mutianyu, with the slide down the toboggan
great-wall.goWhen: April to June and September to November; bundle up, the wind is cold

chengdu.blurb: Sichuan's capital and the place Chinese people go to eat, in a city that runs on teahouses and a pace notably slower than the coast. The giant panda bases are genuinely worth a morning, and the Sichuan cooking here is the reason most visitors come.
bestFor: Sichuan hotpot with a local's ordering
The giant panda breeding bases at opening
chengdu.goWhen: March to June and September to November

seoul.blurb: Korea's capital, split by a river and ringed by mountains, with a palace culture that rebuilt itself four times and a food culture that runs from market stalls to Michelin rooms. The mountains are inside the city and public, which almost no other capital can say.
seoul.goWhen: April to June and September to November; December is cold but the winter palaces are the draw

tokyo.blurb: The largest city on earth, organised by rail rather than by street, with something genuinely new in a different district every time anyone goes. It is also the only capital where a 14-seat restaurant is a national treasure and a legal art form.
bestFor: Day trips to Hakone and Kamakura
tokyo.goWhen: Late March to April for cherry blossom; October and November for the mildest weather

kyoto.blurb: Japan's former capital, and the only city where the imperial palace, the geisha districts and the temple gardens all still function as living things rather than exhibits. The best time to be there is not cherry blossom season, which is when everyone else is there.
bestFor: Winter or late autumn, between seasons
kyoto.goWhen: Late November and December, or the second half of May

okinawa.blurb: Japan's subtropical islands, a short flight from Tokyo and a completely different climate and culture from the mainland. The reef is the draw, the food is Okinawan and heavy on pork and bitter melon, and the language Ryukyuan is not Japanese at all.
bestFor: Ryukyu cooking: tonkotsu and bitter melon
The peace parks at the war sites
okinawa.goWhen: May to June and October; the typhoon season is June to October and the water is at its clearest in May

tohoku.blurb: Japan's northeast, which is the part of the country the 2011 earthquake and tsunami hit hardest, and which has spent fifteen years rebuilding and reopening. Aomori's nebuta, Yamagata's snow country, and the Sanriku coast's recovery are a visit nobody has made since.
tohoku.goWhen: July to September for hiking, February to March for snow country

taiwan.blurb: An island of night markets, hot springs, and the best trail running anywhere, where the railways, temples and Indigenous towns are all one easy trip. Tainan is the food capital of the island and one of the best food cities in Asia.
bestFor: Jiufen and the old gold towns
taiwan.goWhen: October to December, and avoid the July to September typhoon season

fulidhoo.blurb: One of the inhabited islands of the Maldives, and the most remote inhabited island in the chain, roughly 600 metres long. It is reachable only by the weekly public ferry, which is why it is the card you are choosing when you choose it.
bestFor: House-reef snorkelling at the edge of the atoll
fulidhoo.goWhen: November to April for the dry northeast monsoon; the ferry runs roughly weekly and weather can cancel it

astana.blurb: Kazakhstan's capital, built almost entirely in the last twenty years on empty steppe, and the newest capital in the world by some measure. It is a deliberate statement about where a landlocked country wants to be, and it is either the most ambitious or the strangest city in Central Asia.
astana.goWhen: May to September; the winter reaches minus 30 and there is a hypertube festival to justify it

sydney.blurb: A harbour city built around one of the natural harbours the world has, with a large circuit of ocean pools that are the actual local swimming culture. The Opera House is the postcard; the pools at dawn are the habit.
bestFor: Coastal walks in Royal National Park
The ferry, which is a cheap harbour tour
sydney.goWhen: October to April; the January summer is hot and the city is on holiday

red-centre.blurb: The red desert centre of the Northern Territory, around Yulara and Uluru, and Australia's most concentrated piece of Indigenous culture and country. Ayers Rock is the least of it: the stars, the tracks and the dot paintings are why people come.
bestFor: The fold art and the night sky
red-centre.goWhen: May to September for the cool dry season; the summer heat exceeds 45

queenstown.blurb: The Southern Hemisphere's adventure capital, in a lakeside basin at the foot of the Remarkables, and New Zealand's most reliable Queenstown is the reason people accept the prices. Milford Sound and the Routeburn are the day trips; the downhill biking is the rest.
queenstown.goWhen: December to March for hiking, June to September for skiing; both book out

dunedin.blurb: New Zealand's southernmost city, a Victorian port town with the steepest street in the country and a large student population, which produces a music and café culture well out of proportion to its size. The Otago Peninsula is wild seabird country within twenty minutes.
bestFor: The steepest street in the world
Speight's and the old city buildings
dunedin.goWhen: December to March; it is a cold wet city in the south

samoa.blurb: The heart of Polynesia, an independent nation that chose not to become a resort destination, and for that reason the fa'a Samoa still runs daily life. The Lalomanu beaches are the country's pride, and the to'ona'i system of the village is a living social structure.
bestFor: Villages where the fiafia runs the day
samoa.goWhen: May to October; the wet season is November to April

new-caledonia.blurb: A French territory in the Pacific and the world's largest barrier reef, with a lagoon that is genuinely a UNESCO natural site. It is a Melanesian island with a French administration, and the mix shows in the food, which is a real argument about what the island is.
bestFor: The UNESCO lagoon and the reef
new-caledonia.goWhen: May to September; the wet season and the cyclone season are the same window

french-polynesia.blurb: French Polynesia: 118 islands and five archipelagos, the most famous of which is Tahiti, which is in fact the least interesting for diving. Bora Bora and Raiatea have the lagoons, and Rangiroa and Fakarava have the reef passes that divers cross the planet for.
bestFor: The remote Tuamotu and Marquesas islands
french-polynesia.goWhen: April and October to November for drier weather; February to March is wet but the reefs are calm

montserrat.blurb: The smallest and most southerly of the Caribbean islands, a British Overseas Territory that lost two thirds of its population to volcanic evacuation between 1995 and 1999. The exclusion zone still covers most of the island, and the part that is open is a genuine adventure destination.
bestFor: Volcano hiking on the Soufrière Hills
Sea and geothermal bathing at the Warm Baths
montserrat.goWhen: December to May; the Atlantic season is drier and the airport is most reliable

new-york.blurb: The city our own home base sits in, and the most misjudged place to be shown around. It is five boroughs, not one, and the neighbourhoods with the good food and the actual daily life are all of a subway ride from wherever you're staying.
bestFor: Neighbourhoods, and the subway between them
The outer boroughs and their ethnic food
Village basement jazz and no booking apps
new-york.goWhen: April to June and September to November; December for the holiday season

miami.blurb: A city built on reclaimed land between two national parks, with a Latin American and Caribbean core that predates the art deco front by a century. Little Havana and Little River are the neighbourhoods worth the drive across town.
bestFor: Little Havana's cafés and domino halls
miami.goWhen: December to March; the summer is humid and hurricane season

maryland.blurb: A small American state between Baltimore and Washington, which is why it has both a working port and the Chesapeake Bay in the same frame. It is a local, unglamorous, genuinely good-to-eat state, and the Bay is the reason to come.
maryland.goWhen: May to June and September to October; the summer is hot and humid

rose-island.blurb: An abandoned prison hospital on a small island in Narragansett Bay, Rhode Island, decommissioned in 1971 and a state park since. The buildings are decaying, the graffiti is extensive, and access is by ferry you book yourself, which is why almost nobody is there.
bestFor: A self-booked ferry and no crowd
rose-island.goWhen: May to September; access is seasonal and the water is genuinely cold

redwoods-parks.blurb: The remaining groves of coast redwood, the tallest trees on earth, in the fog belt along the California coast north of San Francisco. The avenue of tall redwoods at Prairie Creek and the canopy walk at Redwood National Park are the ones everyone should see once.
bestFor: The Prairie Creek avenue and the canopy walk
The fog, which is the point
redwoods-parks.goWhen: June to September; the groves close in winter storms and the fog is thickest in summer

northeastern-minnesota.blurb: The far north of the American Midwest, on the Canadian border, where the Boundary Waters and a working forest economy sit side by side. It is the part of the United States that feels like Canada with better coffee, and it is empty in the way that is genuinely restorative.
bestFor: Wolf and bear country in fall
northeastern-minnesota.goWhen: June to September for paddling, September to October for colour and moose

alaska.blurb: The far northwest of North America, where glaciers reach the sea, Denali is still measured rather than simply climbed, and Southeast Alaska is temperate rainforest with towns you reach by floatplane. Anchorage is a base, not a destination.
bestFor: Denali, and the road into it
Southeast Alaska by ferry and floatplane
The Alaskan Highway north from Yukon
alaska.goWhen: June to August; the light is permanent and every lodge and ferry is booked

new-mexico.blurb: High desert between two mountain ranges, where the light is the reason artists came and the reason they stayed. Santa Fe and Taos are the centres, and the national parks around them have some of the most legible skies in the United States.
bestFor: White Sands, which is genuinely strange
The Perseid meteor shower in August
new-mexico.goWhen: April to June and September to October; the summer monsoon is dramatic and the winter is cold

havana.blurb: A Caribbean capital of colonial plazas, Soviet-era blocks and a music tradition that is genuinely a way of life rather than a performance for visitors. The city is a complicated place to be, and the live music is real in a way few places can match.
bestFor: Cuban art and film at the ICAIC

quebec.blurb: Canada's only French-speaking province, which is a different country in practice: a distinct cuisine, a distinct accent, and a medieval walled capital that survives inside a modern North American country. Old Québec in winter is one of the great images.
bestFor: Poutine and the market on rue Saint-Paul
quebec.goWhen: June to October, or February for the winter festival

prince-edward-island.blurb: Canada's smallest province, a low green island of red soil, lobster and sand dunes, mostly farm fields and coastal villages. The famous things are the Anne of Green Gable house, and the reason people come is everything else about it.
bestFor: The red sand beaches and dunes
prince-edward-island.goWhen: June to September; the Island Music Festival is July

cartagena.blurb: A walled Spanish colonial city on the Caribbean coast of Colombia, with a walled city that is genuinely intact and a city outside the walls that is the real one. The old town's streets are loud, hot and crowded; the Getsemaní and Bocagrande beyond them are the locals' city.
bestFor: Playa de la mercy for the sunset
cartagena.goWhen: December to April; the wet season is May to November

galapagos-islands.blurb: The Galápagos, where species evolved in isolation and most exist nowhere else, and where a visitor is a walking biosphere, an introduction and an insurance premium. Overland and cruise routes see different animals because they see different islands.
bestFor: The Galápagos marine reserve's sharks and reef
A licensed naturalist guide, which is required
galapagos-islands.goWhen: December to May for seas and prices; August to November is less windy

machu-picchu.blurb: A fifteenth-century Inca estate on a ridge 2,430 metres up, built without mortar and largely invisible from the approach below. Entry is on timed tickets with a train or a multi-day trek, and the two routes feel like entirely different visits.
bestFor: First bus to the gate, first entry
The Inca Bridge and the Sun Gate on the trek
The terraces and the Temple of the Sun
A dawn on the ridge with no rain
machu-picchu.goWhen: April to October for a clear sky; June to August is wettest and greenest

rio-de-janeiro.blurb: A city set in a granite bay under a statue of Christ, with a beach culture, a samba culture and a serious problem, all present simultaneously. The trick is knowing which beach you are on: Copacabana is a parade, Ipanema is a neighbourhood, and there are seventeen others.
bestFor: Ipanema and Leblon rather than Copacabana
Samba on a Tuesday night in Santa Teresa
Santa Teresa's bars and the views
The cable car up to Sugarloaf
rio-de-janeiro.goWhen: December to March; October to March is summer, and some weeks are 40 degrees

amazon-rainforest.blurb: The Amazon basin, which holds roughly a tenth of all species on earth, and which is not a tourist destination so much as a set of ways to be in one. Manaus is the main gateway; the Anavilhanas archipelago and the Tambopata and Madidi reserves are the real forest.
bestFor: Flooded forest by canoe in Anavilhanas
Night walks for genuinely different wildlife
Birds — more species than anywhere on earth
Being honest about what tourism supports
amazon-rainforest.goWhen: May to September for the dry season; the flooded forest peaks around June

salar-de-uyuni.blurb: The largest salt flat on earth, at 10,000 square kilometres, which is a mirror when there is water on it and a blinding white void when there is not. It is genuinely one of the most strange landscapes anywhere, and the cactus-covered islands on it are its only landmarks.
bestFor: The mirror season, roughly April to June
Cactus islands on the salt crust
The fumaroles and geysers at Sol de Mana
salar-de-uyuni.goWhen: December to March for the mirror; June to August for the geysers

buenos-aires.blurb: A southern capital built on a river delta with a genuinely European feel and a genuinely Latin American appetite. Milongas, bookshops in former theatres, and a steak culture that is a national religion rather than a marketing category.
bestFor: A milonga, which is a different thing from a tango show
La Boca and the Caminito murals
The market and the parrilla of beef
buenos-aires.goWhen: October to March; the summer is hot and muggy

bariloche.blurb: A Patagonian lake town in the Argentine Andes, built by a mistake, and now a serious food and craft destination as well as a skiing one. The lake, the chocolate, the chocolate, and the trout fishing are the four reasons.
bestFor: The lake and the Circuito Chico
Skiing in winter, hiking in summer
Drinking craft beer in an old brewery
bariloche.goWhen: December to March for hiking, June to September for skiing; April is the fall colours

torres-del-paine.blurb: A national park at the far end of Patagonia where three granite towers, a turquoise lake and glaciers of the Southern Ice Field share one frame. It's a full multi-day trek or a day walk into the base of the towers, and there is no cheap way to see it.
bestFor: The base of the towers in a day, if it is clear
The W trek, five days, no substitute
torres-del-paine.goWhen: November to March; the wind is genuinely serious and the light is extraordinary

leon.blurb: Nicaragua's original Spanish city, colonial, hot, and largely bypassed by the tourism that went to Granada on the other side of the lake. Its festival is one of the loudest in the Americas, and the surrounding volcanoes are still active.
leon.goWhen: November to April; the Caribbean coast rain arrives in June

monteverde.blurb: The original cloud forest reserve, on the Cordillera de Tilarán in Costa Rica, and one of the first ecotourism projects anywhere. The hanging bridges are a fraction of the area; the reserve's zones and the night walks are the reason to come at all.
bestFor: The cloud forest reserve and its bridges
Night walks for quetzals and frogs
The nearby springs and the river
monteverde.goWhen: December to April for the dry season; the cloud forest is misty year-round

bocas-del-toro.blurb: A Caribbean archipelago in Panama of roughly 90 islands, best known for the Colón reef where the Smithsonian Research Institute has studied coral spawning since 1978, and for the Isla Solarte surf that has its own town. The standard tour drops you in the wrong town on the wrong island, so go to Solarte.
bestFor: Isla Solarte surf and the reef
Staying several nights rather than one day trip
bocas-del-toro.goWhen: December to April, and February to May for the whale sharks nearby

valle-de-guadalupe.blurb: A valley half an hour from Tijuana, full of wineries, olive oil and restaurants run by people who left the city's restaurants, which is what gives it its reputation. It has become a serious food destination on the strength of produce and altitude rather than investment.
bestFor: The Baja wine valley's own region
Sea, surf and food in one day
valle-de-guadalupe.goWhen: March to November; the summer heat is fine here but the restaurants book ahead

antarctic-peninsula.blurb: The 1,200-kilometre finger of Antarctica that reaches toward South America, and the part of the continent you can land on: penguin colonies, calving glaciers, seals and whales, from a Zodiac or a small ship. There is no other way to be here and no reason to hurry.
bestFor: Whale watching in the Falklands season
antarctic-peninsula.goWhen: November to March; the season is short and the weather sets the itinerary
